abstract: In living plant cells, salt affects cell wall architecture directly and triggers diverse cellular responses that, in turn, feed back on wall organization and deposition. These intertwined effects obscure whether salt directly alters wall mechanical properties and thereby influences turgor-driven wall enlargement, the process underlying cell growth. In this study, we studied the tensile mechanical behavior of isolated cell wall materials at physiologically relevant salt concentrations. NaCl induced a small, reversible deformation without significantly altering the apparent axial tensile stiffness of hypocotyl walls. However, salt directly and reversibly inhibited acid-induced wall creep. Similar inhibition was observed in distinct cell wall types and in living Arabidopsis hypocotyls. Assays combining -expansin extracts with cellulose filter paper further supported direct inhibition of wall-loosening activity by salt. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested a mechanism in which Na electrostatically perturbs the conserved active-site Asp and its associated hydrogen-bond network. Together, these findings indicate that salt directly inhibits acid growth by suppressing -expansin-mediated wall creep, highlighting expansin as a physicochemical transducer linking environmental salinity to growth regulation.
